plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes connected to the Weakness node representing CWE-522 via the EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship. Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.

For each AttackPattern identified in q1, find all TaxonomyEntry nodes reachable via MAPS_TO where the taxonomy is ATT&CK (taxonomy_name = 'ATTACK'). Return the entry_id (ATT&CK technique/sub-technique id) for each mapping.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, find all Mitigation nodes reachable via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation descriptions.

For each ATT&CK technique/sub-technique id obtained from q2 (via the attack-technique-id join), retrieve the corresponding Technique or SubTechnique node and all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES. Return technique name, id, and mitigation descriptions.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes connected to the Weakness node representing CWE-287 via the EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship. Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.

For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy is ATT&CK (taxonomy_name = 'ATTACK'). Return the entry_id values (ATT&CK technique/sub-technique IDs) and the TaxonomyEntry details.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the HAS_MITIGATION relationship. Return mitigation names and descriptions.

Find all Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK IDs obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings in q2 (e.g., T1003, T1003.006). Return technique names, IDs, and parent tactic.
For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q4, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship. Return mitigation names and descriptions.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

CAPEC-7 (Blind SQL Injection): Blind SQL Injection results from an insufficient mitigation for SQL Injection. Although suppressing database error messages are considered best practice, the suppression alone is not sufficient to prevent SQL Injection. Blind SQL Injection is a form of SQL Injection that overcomes the lack of error messages. Without the error messages that facilitate SQL Injection, the adversary constructs input strings that probe the target through simple Boolean SQL expressions. The adversary can determine if the syntax and structure of the injection was successful based on whether the query was executed or not.

Executable Blocking:

- Use Case: Prevent execution of binaries from suspicious locations, such as `%TEMP%` or `%APPDATA%` directories.
- Implementation: Block execution of `.exe`, `.bat`, or `.ps1` files from user-writable directories.

Dynamic Analysis Prevention:
- Use Case: Use behavior-based execution prevention tools to identify and block malicious activity in real time.
- Implemenation: Employ EDR solutions that analyze runtime behavior and block suspicious code execution..

T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery) description: Adversaries may delete or remove built-in data and turn off services designed to aid in the recovery of a corrupted system to prevent recovery.(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018)(Citation: FireEye WannaCry 2017) This may deny access to available backups and recovery options. Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may disable or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of [Data Destruction](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1485) and [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486).(Citation: Talos Olympic Destroyer 2018)(Citation: FireEye WannaCry 2017) Furthermore, adversaries may disable recovery notifications, then corrupt backups.(Citation: disable_notif_synology_ransom) A number of native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features: * vssadmin.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system - vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet * [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047) can be used to delete volume shadow copies - wmic shadowcopy delete * wbadmin.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog - wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet * bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data - bcdedit.exe /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no * REAgentC.exe can be used to disable Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) repair/recovery options of an infected system * diskshadow.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system - diskshadow delete shadows all (Citation: Diskshadow) (Citation: Crytox Ransomware) On network devices, adversaries may leverage [Disk Wipe](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1561) to delete backup firmware images and reformat the file system, then [System Shutdown/Reboot](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1529) to reload the device. Together this activity may leave network devices completely inoperable and inhibit recovery operations. On ESXi servers, adversaries may delete or encrypt snapshots of virtual machines to support [Data Encrypted for Impact](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486), preventing them from being leveraged as backups (e.g., via ` vim-cmd vmsvc/snapshot.removeall`).(Citation: Cybereason) Adversaries may also delete “online” backups that are connected to their network – whether via network storage media or through folders that sync to cloud services.(Citation: ZDNet Ransomware Backups 2020) In cloud environments, adversaries may disable versioning and backup policies and delete snapshots, database backups, machine images, and prior versions of objects designed to be used in disaster recovery scenarios.(Citation: Dark Reading Code Spaces Cyber Attack)(Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS S3 Ransomware).

gold_question: How is T1047 (Windows Management Instrumentation) detected, and via which analytics?
note: paraphrase of name idea, no id/name/avoid words

plan.text: Find Technique and SubTechnique nodes representing built-in Windows administrative interfaces used for command execution (e.g., PowerShell, Windows Command Shell, WMI) — the adversary abusing a native Windows shell or scripting interface to run commands.

For each DetectionStrategy that DETECTS the techniques identified in q1, retrieve the DetectionStrategy, every Analytic linked via HAS_ANALYTIC, and every DataComponent that each Analytic MONITORS. Return the strategy name, analytic description, and the specific log-source / observable data components a defender would inspect.

Find AttackPattern nodes whose TaxonomyEntry (MAPS_TO, taxonomy_name=ATTACK) entry_id matches the ATT&CK technique IDs from q1, and for each such AttackPattern retrieve all associated Indicator nodes (HAS_INDICATOR). Return the indicator descriptions that describe observable signs a defender would see.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

Return the CAPEC id, name, and any associated TaxonomyEntry mapping to ATT&CK.

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

CAPEC-7 (Blind SQL Injection): Blind SQL Injection results from an insufficient mitigation for SQL Injection. Although suppressing database error messages are considered best practice, the suppression alone is not sufficient to prevent SQL Injection. Blind SQL Injection is a form of SQL Injection that overcomes the lack of error messages. CAPEC-150 (Collect Data from Common Resource Locations): An adversary exploits well-known locations for resources for the purposes of undermining the security of the target. In many, if not most systems, files and resources are organized in a default tree structure. This can be useful for adversaries because they often know where to look for resources or files that are necessary for attacks. Even when the precise location of a targeted resource may not be known, naming conventions may indicate a small area of the target machine's file tree where the resources are typically located. For example, configuration files are normally stored in the /etc director on Unix systems. Adversaries can take advantage of this to commit other types of attacks.

plan.text: Find AttackPattern(s) whose description matches 'guessing or riding along on a trusted token, such as a session ID or cookie, to act as though you were an already-authenticated user' (session hijacking / session fixation type patterns). For each matching AttackPattern, follow MAPS_TO to TaxonomyEntry nodes where taxonomy_name is 'ATTACK' and return the mapped entry_id (the ATT&CK technique ID).
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION, including their descriptions.

Find Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the entry_id values supplied from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mapping (T-prefixed IDs such as T1003.006, T1484.001, etc.). Return the technique name, description, and any associated Tactic via HAS_TACTIC.
For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q3, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES, including mitigation name and description.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000

plan.text: Find all Techniques and SubTechniques whose names or descriptions relate to hijacking, stealing, reusing, or piggybacking on session tokens, application access tokens, security tokens, OAuth tokens, or other authentication material to impersonate a verified user or service (e.g., Use Alternate Authentication Material, Steal Application Access Token, and their sub-techniques).

T1550.003 (Pass the Ticket): Adversaries may “pass the ticket” using stolen Kerberos tickets to move laterally within an environment, bypassing normal system access controls. Pass the ticket (PtT) is a method of authenticating to a system using Kerberos tickets without having access to an account's password. Kerberos authentication can be used as the first step to lateral movement to a remote system.

queries: MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Analytic OR n:Campaign OR n:DataComponent OR n:DetectionStrategy OR n:Group OR n:Matrix OR n:Mitigation OR n:Software OR n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) AND any(term IN $names WHERE toLower(n.name) CONTAINS term) WITH collect(n) AS cand WITH cand, [x IN cand WHERE any(t IN $names WHERE toLower(x.name) = t)] AS exact UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(exact) > 0 THEN exact ELSE cand END) AS n OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

MATCH (n:DetectionStrategy) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 1000

gold_question: Which ATT&CK tactics do the techniques mapped from CAPEC-565 (Password Spraying) belong to?
note: built entirely from the description of cycling common passwords across many accounts

plan.text: Find the AttackPattern(s) that best describe an approach in which an attacker tries a short list of commonly used passwords against many different user accounts, moving on to a new account before repeating any password, in order to uncover valid credentials (i.e., password spraying / credential stuffing / cross-account password guessing). Return the matching AttackPattern node(s) and any associated TaxonomyEntry that maps to an external taxonomy.

For each ATT&CK Technique or SubTechnique node identified via the attack-technique-id join from the CAPEC result, retrieve the Tactic node(s) to which it belongs (i.e., the broad phase of the intrusion such as Initial Access, Credential Access, Lateral Movement, etc.).

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

T1606 (Forge Web Credentials): Adversaries may forge credential materials that can be used to gain access to web applications or Internet services. Web applications and services (hosted in cloud SaaS environments or on-premise servers) often use session cookies, tokens, or other materials to authenticate and authorize user access.

Adversaries may generate these credential materials in order to gain access to web resources. This differs from Steal Web Session Cookie, Steal Application Access Token, and other similar behaviors in that the credentials are new and forged by the adversary, rather than stolen or intercepted from legitimate users.

gold_question: Which ATT&CK tactics do the techniques mapped from CAPEC-633 (Token Impersonation) belong to?
note: paraphrased the name as forging an impersonating credential; no id, no exact name, no avoid words

plan.text: Identify the Technique or SubTechnique that describes forging an authentication credential that poses as someone else (e.g., Forge Web Credentials, Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets, or any other credential-forging technique where the attacker impersonates another identity).

For each Technique or SubTechnique identified in q1, retrieve all associated Tactic nodes via the HAS_TACTIC relationship to determine which broad phases of an intrusion (e.g., Credential Access, Defense Evasion, Lateral Movement) they fall under.

queries: MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Analytic OR n:Campaign OR n:DataComponent OR n:DetectionStrategy OR n:Group OR n:Matrix OR n:Mitigation OR n:Software OR n:SubTechnique OR n:Tactic OR n:Technique) AND any(term IN $names WHERE toLower(n.name) CONTAINS term) WITH collect(n) AS cand WITH cand, [x IN cand WHERE any(t IN $names WHERE toLower(x.name) = t)] AS exact UNWIND (CASE WHEN size(exact) > 0 THEN exact ELSE cand END) AS n OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]-(m) WITH n, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE type(r) END AS rel, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE startNode(r) = n END AS outgoing, CASE WHEN m IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE head(labels(m)) END AS neighbour_label, count(m) AS cnt WITH n, collect(CASE WHEN rel IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE {rel: rel, outgoing: outgoing, label: neighbour_label, count: cnt} END) AS raw WITH n, [f IN raw WHERE f IS NOT NULL] AS facets RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name, n.properties_json AS properties_json, facets AS facets LIMIT 50

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000
MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t:Technique) RETURN ta.attack_id AS tactic_id, ta.name AS tactic_name, t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name LIMIT 100

T1040 (Network Sniffing) description: Adversaries may passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network. Network sniffing refers to using the network interface on a system to monitor or capture information sent over a wired or wireless connection. An adversary may place a network interface into promiscuous mode to passively access data in transit over the network, or use span ports to capture a larger amount of data.

Data captured via this technique may include user credentials, especially those sent over an insecure, unencrypted protocol. Techniques for name service resolution poisoning, such as [Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/001), can also be used to capture credentials to websites, proxies, and internal systems by redirecting traffic to an adversary.

Network sniffing may reveal configuration details, such as running services, version numbers, and other network characteristics (e.g. IP addresses, hostnames, VLAN IDs) necessary for subsequent [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and/or [Stealth](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0005) activities. Adversaries may likely also utilize network sniffing during [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) (AiTM) to passively gain additional knowledge about the environment.

In cloud-based environments, adversaries may still be able to use traffic mirroring services to sniff network traffic from virtual machines. For example, AWS Traffic Mirroring, GCP Packet Mirroring, and Azure vTap allow users to define specified instances to collect traffic from and specified targets to send collected traffic to.(Citation: AWS Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: GCP Packet Mirroring)(Citation: Azure Virtual Network TAP) Often, much of this traffic will be in cleartext due to the use of TLS termination at the load balancer level to reduce the strain of encrypting and decrypting traffic.(Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: SpecterOps AWS Traffic Mirroring) The adversary can then use exfiltration techniques such as Transfer Data to Cloud Account in order to access the sniffed traffic.(Citation: Rhino Security Labs AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring)

On network devices, adversaries may perform network captures using [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) commands such as `monitor capture`.(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: capture_embedded_packet_on_software).

T1566 (Phishing) description: Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. All forms of phishing are electronically delivered social engineering. Phishing can be targeted, known as spearphishing. In spearphishing, a specific individual, company, or industry will be targeted by the adversary. More generally, adversaries can conduct non-targeted phishing, such as in mass malware spam campaigns.

Adversaries may send victims emails containing malicious attachments or links, typically to execute malicious code on victim systems. Phishing may also be conducted via third-party services, like social media platforms. Phishing may also involve social engineering techniques, such as posing as a trusted source, as well as evasive techniques such as removing or manipulating emails or metadata/headers from compromised accounts being abused to send messages (e.g., [Email Hiding Rules](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/008)).(Citation: Microsoft OAuth Spam 2022)(Citation: Palo Alto Unit 42 VBA Infostealer 2014) Another way to accomplish this is by [Email Spoofing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1684/002)(Citation: Proofpoint-spoof) the identity of the sender, which can be used to fool both the human recipient as well as automated security tools,(Citation: cyberproof-double-bounce) or by including the intended target as a party to an existing email thread that includes malicious files or links (i.e., "thread hijacking").(Citation: phishing-krebs)

Victims may also receive phishing messages that instruct them to call a phone number where they are directed to visit a malicious URL, download malware,(Citation: sygnia Luna Month)(Citation: CISA Remote Monitoring and Management Software) or install adversary-accessible remote management tools onto their computer (i.e., [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204)).(Citation: Unit42 Luna Moth).

gold_question: Which CAPEC patterns map to ATT&CK technique T1110.001 (Password Guessing), and what is that technique?
note: paraphrased the name as repeatedly trying passwords without inside knowledge

plan.text: Find the Technique and SubTechnique entries that describe repeatedly trying different passwords against an account without any inside knowledge of the real password (brute-force / password guessing). Return the technique name, description, associated Tactic, and any HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE children so the full method is captured.

Find all AttackPattern nodes that have a MAPS_TO relationship to a TaxonomyEntry whose taxonomy_name is 'ATTACK' and whose entry_id matches the ATT&CK technique/sub-technique ID(s) returned by q1. Return the AttackPattern name, description, and the linking TaxonomyEntry.

For each AttackPattern identified in q2, retrieve its ExecutionSteps, Prerequisites, Resources, Skills, Consequences, Indicators, and Mitigations to provide a full breakdown of what the method actually involves from the CAPEC perspective.

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 100
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(100)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(200)

plan.text: Find the Technique whose description matches 'logging into a system over a remote connection with valid login credentials' (e.g., Valid Accounts / remote authentication with valid credentials). Find all AttackPattern nodes that have a MAPS_TO relationship to a TaxonomyEntry where taxonomy_name is 'ATTACK', and retrieve each matching AttackPattern's description, its ExecutionStep children (via HAS_EXECUTION_STEP), and the TaxonomyEntry entry_id so the mapping to the specific ATT&CK technique can be confirmed.

queries: MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, ta.attack_id AS in_tactic_id, ta.name AS in_tactic_name LIMIT 1000

gold_question: Which CAPEC patterns exploit weakness CWE-294, which ATT&CK techniques do they map to, and what mitigations apply?
note: schema words replaced with plain phrasing

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node representing CWE-294. Return the AttackPattern id, name, and description.
For the AttackPatterns identified in q1, retrieve their MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy is ATT&CK, to obtain the corresponding ATT&CK technique/sub-technique ids.
Retrieve the Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK ids obtained from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry mappings in q2. Return technique name, description, and tactic associations.
For the AttackPatterns identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes linked via HAS_MITIGATION. Return mitigation name and description.
For the Technique and SubTechnique nodes retrieved in q3, find all Mitigation nodes that have a MITIGATES relationship to them. Return mitigation name and description.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t:Technique) RETURN ta.attack_id AS tactic_id, ta.name AS tactic_name, t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().has("id", within(ids)).project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

note: dash-fragment sentence shape

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to a Weakness node representing CWE-308. For each such AttackPattern, also retrieve its TaxonomyEntry mappings via MAPS_TO where the taxonomy is ATT&CK (to expose the ATT&CK technique id for joining).

Retrieve Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id matches the ATT&CK ids supplied from the CAPEC TaxonomyEntry join (attack-technique-id). Return the technique name, id, and any associated Tactic via HAS_TACTIC.
For the AttackPattern nodes identified in q1 (those exploiting CWE-308), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION, including the mitigation description.

For the Technique and SubTechnique nodes identified in q2 (reached via the attack-technique-id join), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES, including the mitigation name and description.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t:Technique) RETURN ta.attack_id AS tactic_id, ta.name AS tactic_name, t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name LIMIT 1000

gold_question: Which CAPEC patterns exploit weakness CWE-521, which ATT&CK techniques do they map to, and what mitigations apply?
note: schema words replaced with plain phrasing

plan.text: Find all AttackPattern nodes that have an EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS relationship to the Weakness node whose identifier is CWE-521. Return the AttackPattern IDs and names.

For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve its MAPS_TO TaxonomyEntry nodes where the taxonomy is ATT&CK (taxonomy_name = 'ATTACK'), returning the entry_id (ATT&CK technique/sub-technique ID) for each mapping.

For the ATT&CK Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose attack_id values match the entry_ids produced by q2, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via MITIGATES, returning mitigation IDs, names, and descriptions.
For each AttackPattern identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION, returning mitigation descriptions and any associated details.

queries: MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 1000
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)
g.V().hasLabel("AttackPattern").project("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

g.V().hasLabel("Weakness").has("id", within(cweIds)).as("w").in("EXPLOITS_WEAKNESS").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").project("w","ap","tax").by(__.select("w").elementMap()).by(__.select("ap").elementMap()).by(__.out("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").elementMap().fold()).limit(1000)

CAPEC-66 (SQL Injection) has 3 mitigations, named only as text: “Strong input validation - All user-controllable input must be validated and filtered for illegal characters as well as SQL content. Keywords such as UNION, SELECT or INSERT must be filtered in addition to characters such as a single-quote(') or SQL-comments (--) based on the context in which they appear.”; “Use of parameterized queries or stored procedures - Parameterization causes the input to be restricted to certain domains, such as strings or integers, and any input outside such domains is considered invalid and the query fails. Note that SQL Injection is possible even in the presence of stored procedures if the eventual query is constructed dynamically.”; “Use of custom error pages - Attackers can glean information about the nature of queries from descriptive error messages. Input validation must be coupled with customized error pages that inform about an error without disclosing information about the database or application.”.

CAPEC-66 (SQL Injection) has 2 weaknesses: CWE-1286, CWE-89.

CAPEC-66 (SQL Injection) has 3 mitigations, named only as text: “Strong input validation - All user-controllable input must be validated and filtered for illegal characters as well as SQL content. Keywords such as UNION, SELECT or INSERT must be filtered in addition to characters such as a single-quote(') or SQL-comments (--) based on the context in which they appear.”; “Use of parameterized queries or stored procedures - Parameterization causes the input to be restricted to certain domains, such as strings or integers, and any input outside such domains is considered invalid and the query fails. Note that SQL Injection is possible even in the presence of stored procedures if the eventual query is constructed dynamically.”; “Use of custom error pages - Attackers can glean information about the nature of queries from descriptive error messages. Input validation must be coupled with customized error pages that inform about an error without disclosing information about the database or application.”.

CAPEC-66 (SQL Injection) has 4 Consequences, named only as text: “Modify Data Integrity”; “Read Data Confidentiality”; “Execute Unauthorized Commands Confidentiality Integrity Availability”; “Gain Privileges Confidentiality Access Control Authorization”.

CAPEC-66 (SQL Injection) has 4 ExecutionSteps, named only as text: “Experiment 2 [Determine user-controllable input susceptible to injection] Determine the user-controllable input susceptible to injection. For each user-controllable input that the attacker suspects is vulnerable to SQL injection, attempt to inject characters that have special meaning in SQL (such as a single quote character, a double quote character, two hyphens, a parenthesis, etc.). The goal is…”; “Experiment 3 [Experiment with SQL Injection vulnerabilities] After determining that a given input is vulnerable to SQL Injection, hypothesize what the underlying query looks like. Iteratively try to add logic to the query to extract information from the database, or to modify or delete information in the database.”; “Exploit 4 [Exploit SQL Injection vulnerability] After refining and adding various logic to SQL queries, craft and execute the underlying SQL query that will be used to attack the target system. The goal is to reveal, modify, and/or delete database data, using the knowledge obtained in the previous step. This could entail crafting and executing multiple SQL queries if a denial of service attack is…”; “Explore 1 [Survey application] The attacker first takes an inventory of the functionality exposed by the application.”.

An attacker crafts input strings so that when the target software constructs SQL statements based on the input, the resulting SQL statement performs actions other than those the application intended. SQL Injection results from failure of the application to appropriately validate input.

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters): Some APIs will strip certain leading characters from a string of parameters. An adversary can intentionally introduce leading "ghost" characters (extra characters that don't affect the validity of the request at the API layer) that enable the input to pass the filters and therefore process the adversary's input. This occurs when the targeted API will accept input data in several syntactic forms and interpret it in the equivalent semantic way, while the filter does not take into account the full spectrum of the syntactic forms acceptable to the targeted API.

CAPEC-3 (Using Leading 'Ghost' Character Sequences to Bypass Input Filters): Some APIs will strip certain leading characters from a string of parameters. An adversary can intentionally introduce leading "ghost" characters (extra characters that don't affect the validity of the request at the API layer) that enable the input to pass the filters and therefore process the adversary's input. claims: CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) description: In applications, particularly web applications, access to functionality is mitigated by an authorization framework. This framework maps Access Control Lists (ACLs) to elements of the application's functionality; particularly URL's for web apps. In the case that the administrator failed to specify an ACL for a particular element, an attacker may be able to access it with impunity. An attacker with the ability to access functionality not properly constrained by ACLs can obtain sensitive information and possibly compromise the entire application. Such an attacker can access resources that must be available only to users at a higher privilege level, can access management sections of the application, or can run queries for data that they otherwise not supposed to..
CAPEC-1 (Accessing Functionality Not Properly Constrained by ACLs) has 1 ATT&CK mapping: T1574.010.

CAPEC-10 (Buffer Overflow via Environment Variables) description: This attack pattern involves causing a buffer overflow through manipulation of environment variables. Once the adversary finds that they can modify an environment variable, they may try to overflow associated buffers. This attack leverages implicit trust often placed in environment variables..

CAPEC-100 (Overflow Buffers) description: Buffer Overflow attacks target improper or missing bounds checking on buffer operations, typically triggered by input injected by an adversary. As a consequence, an adversary is able to write past the boundaries of allocated buffer regions in memory, causing a program crash or potentially redirection of execution as per the adversaries' choice..

CAPEC-101 (Server Side Include (SSI) Injection) description: An attacker can use Server Side Include (SSI) Injection to send code to a web application that then gets executed by the web server. Doing so enables the attacker to achieve similar results to Cross Site Scripting, viz., arbitrary code execution and information disclosure, albeit on a more limited scale, since the SSI directives are nowhere near as powerful as a full-fledged scripting language. Nonetheless, the attacker can conveniently gain access to sensitive files, such as password files, and execute shell commands..

CAPEC-102 (Session Sidejacking) description: Session sidejacking takes advantage of an unencrypted communication channel between a victim and target system. The attacker sniffs traffic on a network looking for session tokens in unencrypted traffic. Once a session token is captured, the attacker performs malicious actions by using the stolen token with the targeted application to impersonate the victim. This attack is a specific method of session hijacking, which is exploiting a valid session token to gain unauthorized access to a target system or information. Other methods to perform a session hijacking are session fixation, cross-site scripting, or compromising a user or server machine and stealing the session token..

CAPEC-628 (Carry-Off GPS Attack) description: A common form of a GPS spoofing attack, commonly termed a carry-off attack begins with an adversary broadcasting signals synchronized with the genuine signals observed by the target receiver. The power of the counterfeit signals is then gradually increased and drawn away from the genuine signals. Over time, the adversary can carry the target away from their intended destination and toward a location chosen by the adversary..

CAPEC-63 (Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)) description: An adversary embeds malicious scripts in content that will be served to web browsers. The goal of the attack is for the target software, the client-side browser, to execute the script with the users' privilege level. An attack of this type exploits a programs' vulnerabilities that are brought on by allowing remote hosts to execute code and scripts. Web browsers, for example, have some simple security controls in place, but if a remote attacker is allowed to execute scripts (through injecting them in to user-generated content like bulletin boards) then these controls may be bypassed. Further, these attacks are very difficult for an end user to detect..

CAPEC-630 (TypoSquatting) description: An adversary registers a domain name with at least one character different than a trusted domain. A TypoSquatting attack takes advantage of instances where a user mistypes a URL (e.g. www.goggle.com) or not does visually verify a URL before clicking on it (e.g. phishing attack). As a result, the user is directed to an adversary-controlled destination. TypoSquatting does not require an attack against the trusted domain or complicated reverse engineering..

CAPEC-631 (SoundSquatting) description: An adversary registers a domain name that sounds the same as a trusted domain, but has a different spelling. A SoundSquatting attack takes advantage of a user's confusion of the two words to direct Internet traffic to adversary-controlled destinations. SoundSquatting does not require an attack against the trusted domain or complicated reverse engineering..

CAPEC-632 (Homograph Attack via Homoglyphs) description: An adversary registers a domain name containing a homoglyph, leading the registered domain to appear the same as a trusted domain. A homograph attack leverages the fact that different characters among various character sets look the same to the user. Homograph attacks must generally be combined with other attacks, such as phishing attacks, in order to direct Internet traffic to the adversary-controlled destinations..

CAPEC-7 (Blind SQL Injection) has 6 execution steps, named only as text: “Explore 2 [Determine how to inject information into the queries] Determine how to inject information into the queries from the previous step such that the injection does not impact their logic. For example, the following are possible injections for those queries: "5' OR 1=1; --" and "5) OR 1=1; --" and "ordernum DESC; --"”; “Experiment 3 [Determine user-controllable input susceptible to injection] Determine the user-controllable input susceptible to injection. For each user-controllable input that the adversary suspects is vulnerable to SQL injection, attempt to inject the values determined in the previous step. If an error does not occur, then the adversary knows that the SQL injection was successful.”; “Experiment 4 [Determine database type] Determines the type of the database, such as MS SQL Server or Oracle or MySQL, using logical conditions as part of the injected queries”; “Exploit 5 [Extract information about database schema] Extract information about database schema by getting the database to answer yes/no questions about the schema.”; “Exploit 6 [Exploit SQL Injection vulnerability] Use the information obtained in the previous steps to successfully inject the database in order to bypass checks or modify, add, retrieve or delete data from the database”; “Explore 1 [Hypothesize SQL queries in application] Generated hypotheses regarding the SQL queries in an application. For example, the adversary may hypothesize that their input is passed directly into a query that looks like: "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ordernum = _____" or "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ordernum IN (_____)" or "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ordernum in (_____) ORDER BY _____" Of cours…”.
CAPEC-7 (Blind SQL Injection) has Abstraction: Detailed; Likelihood_Of_Attack: High; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: High.

CAPEC-7 (Blind SQL Injection): Blind SQL Injection results from an insufficient mitigation for SQL Injection. Although suppressing database error messages are considered best practice, the suppression alone is not sufficient to prevent SQL Injection. Blind SQL Injection is a form of SQL Injection that overcomes the lack of error messages. Without the error messages that facilitate SQL Injection, the adversary constructs input strings that probe the target through simple Boolean SQL expressions. The adversary can determine if the syntax and structure of the injection was successful based on whether the query was executed or not.

CAPEC-16 (Dictionary-based Password Attack) has Abstraction: Detailed; Likelihood_Of_Attack: Medium; Status: Draft; Typical_Severity: High.

CAPEC-16 (Dictionary-based Password Attack): An attacker tries each of the words in a dictionary as passwords to gain access to the system via some user's account. If the password chosen by the user was a word within the dictionary, this attack will be successful (in the absence of other mitigations). This is a specific instance of the password brute forcing attack pattern. Dictionary Attacks differ from similar attacks such as Password Spraying (CAPEC-565) and Credential Stuffing (CAPEC-600), since they leverage unknown username/password combinations and don't care about inducing account lockouts.

plan.text: Identify the Technique and SubTechnique nodes that correspond to each of the three described adversary behaviors: (a) embedding or inserting one script inside another so it executes covertly alongside the host script; (b) inserting executable or runnable code into file types not designed to execute code, such as image files or configuration files; (c) hiding malicious code in unused padding, dead instruction space, or leftover bytes within a compiled library or binary. For each matched technique/sub-technique, also retrieve its parent Tactic via HAS_TACTIC for context.

For each Technique and SubTechnique identified in q1, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship, so the results can be combined into a single deduplicated set of countermeasures covering all three behaviors.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000
MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t:Technique) RETURN ta.attack_id AS tactic_id, ta.name AS tactic_name, t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name LIMIT 1000
question: Since these three approaches overlap — hiding one script inside another so it quietly runs too, sneaking runnable code into files that aren't meant to run any code themselves (like an image or configuration file), and slipping a virus into leftover padding inside a compiled library's instructions — which adversary behaviors would each line up with, and what combined set of countermeasures would help?

plan.text: Identify the three CAPEC attack patterns matching: (1) a script hidden inside another script that a target program is likely to execute, enabled by a remote-code-execution flaw; (2) a system that trusts its own configuration or resource files, so that loading an altered image or settings file causes hidden code to run or the running process to be hijacked; (3) tampering with a compiled library by planting a virus in the padding gaps left between legitimate instructions by compiler optimizations, infecting anything that later links against that library. For each pattern, retrieve its ExecutionSteps, Prerequisites, Resources, Skills, Weaknesses, Indicators, Consequences, Mitigations, and Examples.

Find the ATT&CK Techniques and SubTechniques that correspond to the three CAPEC attack patterns identified in q1 (script-injection via remote code execution; configuration/resource-file trust exploitation; compiled-library padding-gap virus implantation). For each matched Technique/SubTechnique, also retrieve its parent Tactic(s).
For the Techniques and SubTechniques identified in q2, retrieve all associated Mitigations (defensive measures that reduce technique risk).
For the Techniques and SubTechniques identified in q2, retrieve all DetectionStrategies and their associated Analytics and DataComponents that monitor for those behaviors.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 1000

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids MATCH (t)<-[:DETECTS]-(d:DetectionStrategy) OPTIONAL MATCH (d)-[:HAS_ANALYTIC]->(a:Analytic) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, d.attack_id AS detection_id, d.name AS detection_name, a.attack_id AS analytic_id, a.name AS analytic_name LIMIT 1000
MATCH (ta:Tactic)-[:HAS_TECHNIQUE]->(t:Technique) WHERE ta.attack_id IN $ids RETURN ta.attack_id AS tactic_id, ta.name AS tactic_name, t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name LIMIT 1000

question: Picture three separate tricks that all end up overlapping in the same place: one hides a script inside another script that a target program is likely to run anyway, thanks to a flaw that lets a remote host run code; another takes advantage of a system trusting its own configuration or resource files, so that when the program loads an altered image or settings file, the hidden code inside runs or the running process gets hijacked; and the third tampers with a compiled library, planting a virus in the leftover gaps left between legitimate instructions by compiler optimizations, so that anything which later interfaces with that library gets infected — which adversary behaviors would each line up with, and what combined set of countermeasures would help?

plan.text: Find all TaxonomyEntry nodes (taxonomy_name = 'ATTACK') that are targets of the MAPS_TO relationship from AttackPattern nodes whose name is 'Subverting Environment Variable Values' OR 'Inclusion of Code in Existing Process'. plan.text: Find Technique and SubTechnique nodes whose names or descriptions correspond to 'Unsecured Credentials' (credentials, account numbers, or sensitive details left embedded in system files, registry, or configuration artifacts) — i.e. the 'digging through a system to uncover sensitive details left embedded inside it' approach. Return the technique id, name, and any sub-technique children.

Find Technique nodes whose names or descriptions correspond to 'Data from Local System' or 'Data from Network Shared Drive' or 'Data from Information Repositories' — i.e. the 'searching through files an application left without proper access controls to find sensitive information hidden inside them' approach. Return the technique id, name, and tactic.

For the techniques and sub-techniques identified in q1 (Unsecured Credentials family) and q2 (Data from Local System / Data from Network Shared Drive / Data from Information Repositories), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship. Return mitigation id, name, and description so a combined countermeasure set can be assembled.

Find AttackPattern nodes that MAPS_TO a TaxonomyEntry with taxonomy_name='ATTACK' whose entry_id matches any of the ATT&CK technique ids identified in q1 and q2 (e.g. T1552, T1552.001, T1552.002, T1005, T1135, T1213). For each matching AttackPattern, retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via HAS_MITIGATION. Return the CAPEC id, name, and each mitigation's description.

MATCH (t:Technique)-[:HAS_SUBTECHNIQUE]->(st:SubTechnique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OR st.attack_id IN $ids RETURN t.attack_id AS parent_id, t.name AS parent_name, st.attack_id AS subtechnique_id, st.name AS subtechnique_name LIMIT 50

gold_question: Which ATT&CK techniques do CAPEC-37, CAPEC-639 map to (they overlap), and what mitigations apply to the deduplicated union?
note: built from both descriptions only, no identifiers/names/avoid words

plan.text: Find the Technique and any SubTechnique whose name or description matches 'Unsecured Credentials' / 'Credentials In Files' — i.e. an adversary inspecting a system for confidential details (account numbers, keys, credentials) left embedded in files, config, or the registry, used as a stepping stone for further access. Return the technique id, name, and any sub-technique ids.

Find the Technique whose name or description matches 'Data from Local System' — i.e. an adversary opening files that an application left without proper access controls and reading through them for sensitive information that was never meant to be exposed. Return the technique id and name.

For the Unsecured Credentials technique (T1552) and its sub-technique Credentials In Files (T1552.001), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship. Return mitigation id, name, and description.
For the Data from Local System technique (T1005), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the MITIGATES relationship. Return mitigation id, name, and description.

Find all AttackPattern nodes that have a MAPS_TO relationship to a TaxonomyEntry where taxonomy_name is 'ATTACK' and entry_id matches any of the ATT&CK technique ids T1552, T1552.001, or T1005. Return the CAPEC attack pattern id, name, and the linked TaxonomyEntry entry_id.

For the CAPEC AttackPattern nodes identified in q5 (those mapping to ATT&CK T1552, T1552.001, or T1005), retrieve all Mitigation nodes connected via the HAS_MITIGATION relationship. Return mitigation name and description.

queries: MATCH (n:Technique) WHERE coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) IN $ids RETURN coalesce(n.attack_id, n.id) AS id, n.name AS name LIMIT 50

MATCH (t) WHERE (t:Technique OR t:SubTechnique) AND t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 200

MATCH (t:Technique) WHERE t.attack_id IN $ids OPTIONAL MATCH (t)<-[:MITIGATES]-(m:Mitigation) RETURN t.attack_id AS technique_id, t.name AS technique_name, m.attack_id AS mitigation_id, m.name AS mitigation_name LIMIT 200

g.V().hasLabel("TaxonomyEntry").has("taxonomy_name","ATTACK").has("entry_id", within(entryIds)).as("tax").in("MAPS_TO").hasLabel("AttackPattern").as("ap").select("ap","tax").by(elementMap()).limit(100)

question: Picture two separate tricks that overlap here: one carefully inspects a system looking for confidential details — account numbers, keys, credentials — that were left embedded inside it, valuable as a stepping stone toward a bigger goal; the other simply opens up files an application left without proper access controls and reads through them looking for whatever sensitive information was never meant to be exposed — which adversary behaviors would each line up with, and what combined set of countermeasures would help?
